lessons.title: Private Credit, P2P Lending and Structured Debt: High Coupons, Real Default Risk

children.text: Imagine two investors each putting ₹10 lakh into the same fast-growing mid-sized company. One buys its shares. The other lends to it at 12% a year. If the company triples in value, the shareholder makes ₹20 lakh and the lender still makes ₹1.2 lakh. If the company collapses, the shareholder loses everything, and the lender may lose most of it too. That lopsided deal sits under every private credit fund, P2P app, invoice discounting platform and high-yield NCD. A 12 to 14% coupon feels like fixed income. It is really a promise with capped upside and real downside, and understanding that shape is the key to this entire corner of alternatives.

body.text: A lender's best case is getting exactly what was promised. Everything else is a loss of some size. High-coupon credit is not safer equity. It is a bet that nothing goes wrong, and the bill for when things do go wrong tends to arrive all at once, in bad years.

body.caption: ₹10 lakh in the same company, one year later: shareholder vs lender at 12% (illustrative)

markDefs.definition: A return pattern with many small, steady gains and occasional large losses. The average can look healthy, but the bad outcomes are much bigger than the good ones.

children.text: In three out of four outcomes, the lender looks like a genius: steady 12%. In the fourth, the lender gives back five years' worth of interest in one go. This return pattern is called
. It is the opposite of the startup power law in the previous lesson, and it is dangerous for a different reason: years of smooth returns build confidence right up until the loss arrives.

Defaults are not spread evenly over time. They cluster when the economy slows, interest rates rise or credit markets freeze. Using the expected-loss approach from Chapter 1 (gross yield minus probability of default × loss given default, minus fees), here is how the credit ladder holds up in a normal year and a stress year.

children.text: In a normal year, higher coupons win. In a stress year, the ranking flips: the AAA bond barely notices, while unsecured P2P lending earns close to nothing. The stress year is also exactly when equities are falling, which is why lower-quality credit fails as a diversifier when you need one.
Where You Stand in the Queue: Seniority and Security

markDefs.definition: The order in which a failed borrower's money is paid out: secured senior lenders first, then unsecured lenders, then subordinated lenders, and shareholders last.

children.text: When a borrower fails, its remaining assets are paid out in a strict order, often called the
. Two loans with the same 12% coupon can have completely different risk depending on where they sit in that queue and whether they are backed by specific assets.

body.caption: A failed company's assets sell for ₹60 crore: who gets what (illustrative)

body.title: Run the waterfall
body.prompt: Using the same claims as the table (₹50 crore secured senior, ₹30 crore unsecured, ₹10 crore subordinated), suppose the assets sell for ₹70 crore instead. What percentage of their claim do the unsecured lenders recover? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Secured senior lenders take their full ₹50 crore first, leaving ₹20 crore. Unsecured lenders are owed ₹30 crore, so they recover ₹20 crore ÷ ₹30 crore ≈ 66.7%. Subordinated lenders and shareholders still get nothing. A ₹10 crore change in asset value doubled the unsecured recovery, which is how sensitive junior lenders are.

body.label: Recovery under India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code
body.value: Roughly a third of admitted claims, on average
body.context: Across resolved cases since the IBC came into force in 2016, creditors have recovered only around a third of what they claimed, often after years of proceedings. Unsecured and junior creditors typically recover far less than that average.

body.title: When a household name's NCDs went bad: DHFL

children.text: Dewan Housing Finance Corporation (DHFL) was one of India's largest housing finance companies. It raised large amounts from retail investors through public NCD issues and deposits, marketed as high-quality, well-rated fixed income. After the 2018 IL&FS crisis froze credit markets, DHFL began defaulting in 2019, and in late 2019 it became the first financial services company referred for insolvency under the IBC. It was eventually taken over by Piramal Group in 2021, with creditors as a group recovering well under half of what they were owed.
The pattern is the one this lesson describes: years of steady coupons, a credit event triggered by the wider market, and a loss far larger than all the extra interest earned.

body.text: Diversification in lending only works across many unrelated borrowers. Twenty invoices from the same company, or ten NCDs from NBFCs lending to the same kind of borrower, can all fail together. And diversification cannot protect you from a stress year that hits every borrower at once.

body.title: Same coupon, different risk
body.question: Two NCDs from the same NBFC both pay 11%. One is secured and senior. The other is unsecured and subordinated. What is the most accurate conclusion?
options: They carry identical risk because the issuer and coupon are the same
The unsecured subordinated NCD is riskier, and at the same coupon it pays nothing extra for that risk
The subordinated NCD is safer because it is repaid first
Neither can lose money because both are rated
body.explanation: In a default, secured senior holders are paid before unsecured and subordinated holders. The subordinated NCD should pay a noticeably higher coupon for that extra risk. At the same 11%, it is simply the worse deal.

body.title: Name the queue
body.textWithBlank: The strict order in which a failed borrower's creditors and shareholders are paid is often called the ___.
body.explanation: Secured senior lenders sit at the top of the waterfall and shareholders at the bottom. Where you sit decides your recovery rate, and recovery rate decides your loss.

body.title: Dr Menon's 13% app
body.scenario: Dr Menon, 49, a surgeon in Kochi, has ₹1.2 crore in investments, mostly equity mutual funds and FDs. A colleague shows him an invoice discounting app offering "13% fixed returns, 90-day tenure, backed by invoices from large companies." He is thinking of moving ₹40 lakh of FDs into it, spread across about eight invoices, most of them from two well-known companies' suppliers.
body.prompt: Using the ideas in this lesson, what should Dr Menon check and consider before he moves the money?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Understand the payoff. The best case is 13%. The downside is losing a large part of the invoice value if a company does not pay or the platform's structure fails. That is negative skew, not fixed income.

2. Check concentration. Eight invoices tied mostly to two companies is not real diversification. If either company delays payments in a stress year, several invoices can fail together.

3. Check seniority and legal structure. Who exactly owes him money: the large company, the supplier, or a special purpose vehicle? Is his claim secured? What happens if the platform itself shuts down?

4. Check regulation. Oversight of invoice discounting products sold to retail investors varies by structure. He should confirm which regulator, if any, oversees this specific product.

5. Compare with the anchor. 13% against FDs at about 7% is a 6-point spread, taxed at his 30% slab. After even modest expected losses, the real pickup is much smaller.

6. Size it. Moving ₹40 lakh, a third of his investments, would replace his safest assets with some of his riskiest. If he wants exposure, a small slice spread across many unrelated counterparties is more prudent, with his FDs left as the anchor.

points: Lending has capped upside and large downside: the best case is getting what was promised, and a default can wipe out years of interest.
This negative skew produces smooth returns for years, which builds false confidence before losses arrive.
Defaults cluster in stress years: in the illustration, P2P lending falls from about 8% to under 1% net, while a AAA bond barely moves.
Seniority and security decide recovery: in the ₹60 crore example, secured lenders get 100%, unsecured 33% and subordinated nothing.
Under India's IBC, creditors have recovered only around a third of admitted claims on average, often after years.
For any high-coupon product, check concentration, seniority, legal structure, regulator, tax and exit before comparing it with an FD.
